# Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing–Guided Optimization of Pacemaker Rate-Response in an Endurance Athlete With Sinus Node Dysfunction

**Authors:** Paishiun Nelson Hsieh; Katherine Falvey; Andreas Kontopidis; Jessica Burr; Mark É. Czeisler; Marius Chukwurah; Katie Stewart; Timothy W. Churchill; James Sawalla Guseh; Eugene H. Chung

**Affiliations:** aCardiovascular Performance Program, Division of Cardiology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | bBoston Scientific, Marlborough, Massachusetts, USA | cHarvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | dBrigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

Athletes with a permanent pacemaker for sinus node dysfunction can experience exercise intolerance related to suboptimal rate-response pacing, often isolated to periods of peak or prolonged effort. Nominal pacemaker rate modulation settings do not recapitulate physiological exercise well.

We present a case of a 70-year-old lifelong runner with implanted permanent pacemaker for sinus node dysfunction presenting with exercise intolerance and dyspnea on exertion. A combined maximum effort cardiopulmonary exercise test with device interrogation produced an optimized pacemaker settings profile which resolved his symptoms.

Highly active patients with sinus node dysfunction depend on rate-response pacing during exercise. Optimized pacemaker function for high intensity sports can relieve symptoms and improve performance. Our case highlights the importance of an athlete-tailored approach combining maximum effort metabolic, exercise, and device testing.

## History of Presentation

A 70-year-old man with a dual-chamber permanent pacemaker (PPM) presented to a sports cardiology clinic for exercise intolerance and loss of appropriate heart rate adaptive pacing. He was a lifelong distance competitive runner and continued to run. His pacemaker was implanted for a diagnosis of age-related sinus node dysfunction. His blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg, and physical examination was unremarkable. His workup before pacemaker implant included a: 1) coronary computed tomography angiography with mild nonobstructive coronary calcifications; 2) transthoracic echocardiogram within normal limits; 3) ambulatory electrocardiogram (ECG) monitor with rare premature ventricular contractions, one 5 beat run of premature ventricular contractions, and no atrial fibrillation; 4) baseline ECG within normal limits; and 5) a cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) significant for a VO2peak of 33.2 mL/kg/min (121% of age-predicted) and no ECG signs of ischemia or exercise-induced arrhythmias.

## Past Medical History

His other medical history was notable for hypothyroidism on maintenance therapy and a right total knee arthroplasty.

## Differential Diagnosis

The patient's symptoms could be explained by several possible causes including supraventricular arrhythmias, upper rate bundle behavior, ectopy, undersensing, lead malfunction, or insufficient rate-response pacing.

## Investigations

He was brought in for a simultaneous treadmill CPET and device interrogation. The initial settings of his Boston Scientific dual-chamber PPM were DDDR mode, a lower rate limit of 50 ppm, maximum tracking rate of 130 ppm, a paced atrioventricular (AV) delay of 140 to 240 milliseconds, sensed AV delay of 135 to 230 milliseconds, and post-ventricular atrial refractory period of 240 to 280 milliseconds. His accelerometer response factor (RF) was 8, activity threshold was medium, reaction time was 30 seconds, and recovery time was 2 minutes. His minute ventilation RF was 8, fitness level was set to active, ventilatory threshold (VeT) was 105 beats/min, and VeT response was 85%. With graded increase of 0.5% incline every 15 second, the patient was able to increase his heart rate to 135 beats/min but became symptomatic and lightheaded, with appropriate A-sensing and V-sensing native conduction throughout (Figure 1). He did not experience premature ventricular contractions, upper rate bundle behavior/aberrancy, or changes in conduction at higher rates. Device testing revealed normal sensing and pacing thresholds with unchanged lead impedance. He was not symptomatic with pacing at high rates during testing. ## Management

To improve his exercise intolerance, the following changes were made to his pacemaker: 1) his heart rate at the VeT setting was changed in his pacemaker to match true measured VeT on his CPET; 2) the RFs of his accelerometer and minute ventilation sensor were both increased, and his accelerometer reaction time was decreased to allow more gradual drift in heart rate; 3) the algorithms (RhythmIQ and AV search+) promoting intrinsic activity were turned off to shift burden of pacing to his pacemaker; and 4) finally, given he was symptomatic at 135 beats/min at peak effort, his maximum sensor rate was increased to 150 bpm and his lower rate was increased to 60 bpm.

After the application of these changes and immediate repeat simultaneous CPET and device interrogation, he began sinus tracking (A-sensing, V-pacing) and at 1 minute reached his new max tracking rate of 150 (A-pacing, V-pacing) (Figure 2). He also reported significant symptom relief without any ectopy. As expected, a follow-up remote transmission revealed increased atrial pacing burden to 4% and acceptable ventricular pacing burden to 10%, reflective of his level of activity and dynamic paced AV delay algorithms.Figure 2Rate-Response Post-Pacemaker Optimization Settings Change(A) Transition to A-sensed, V-paced at heart rate of 100 beats/min. ## Outcome and Follow-Up

After these changes, he was able to complete a 3.2 km run at maximum tracking rate without any exercise-associated symptoms. Several months later, he submitted heart rate monitoring from a personal wearable exhibiting periodic dips in heart rate, which he reliably reported occurred while running up and down hills.

This was hypothesized to be due to change in thoracic impedances with postural change and altered breathing patterns, as the PPM pulse generator was not fixed to underlying tissue to prevent migration. His blended sensor was adjusted to be accelerometer predominant. As previously shown, a repeat heart rate recording over the same terrain after his blended sensor was adjusted showed resolution of his inappropriate drops in heart rate (Figure 3).Figure 3Wearable Heart Rate Monitoring After Permanent Pacemaker Optimization(A) An approximately 40-minute recording of the patient's heart rate with dips reported to be while running up and down hills. (B) A second 40-minute recording over the same terrain after adjustment of blended sensor. Red arrowheads indicate patient-reported symptoms on hills. ## Discussion

Normal augmentation of cardiac output during exercise primarily relies on increases in heart rate, which generally has a linear relationship to work.1 For patients with sinus node dysfunction, rate-response pacing systems attempt to transduce physiological signals of cardiovascular demand into elevated pacing rates.2 Today, pacemakers commonly use accelerometer-based sensors to detect early vibration using piezoelectric/piezoresistive materials or impedance sensing for measurement of respiratory rate or myocardial contractility, as proxies for physical activity and exercise. However, given the complexity of replicating native sinus node function, these systems are imperfect and require methodical, iterative programming, often customized to specific situations or activities. This is notable in athletes, who may be anticipated to routinely strive for higher maximum heart rates and therefore experience a disproportionate degree of chronotropic incompetence.

Past studies have evaluated the impact of rate-modulated pacing on quality of life and exercise capacity with equivocal results.3, 4, 5 In the ADEPT (Advanced Elements of Pacing Randomized Controlled) trial of 872 patients with PPM for chronotropic incompetence, rate modulation did not increase time walked on a treadmill test.4 By comparison, the DUSISLOG (Dual Sensor vs Single Sensor comparison using patient activity LOGbook) study of 105 patients randomized to dual-sensor or single-sensor pacing showed that although there was no significant difference in quality of life or physical activity between sensor type, 6-minute walking time and questionnaires of quality of life and physical activity all showed improvement when compared with DDD only pacing.5 A more recent study of 501 patients randomized to DDD or DDDR with accelerometer alone or blended sensor showed improvements in heart rate score, a surrogate measure used to predict mortality in patients with implantable cardioverter defibrillators and cardiac resynchronization therapy with defibrillations.6 However, no studies of rate-modulated pacing have included conditioned patients, much less athletes.

Several considerations exist regarding pacemaker programming in athletes with sinus node dysfunction. Accelerometer-based sensors sense mechanical stress agnostic to cause; thus, they function well with repetitive impact activity (eg, running) but underpace with nonimpact rhythmic locomotion (eg, cycling), at very high workloads and during recovery. They can also inappropriately sense mechanical activity unrelated to exercise. Minute ventilation sensors theoretically provide data on the respiratory cycle; however, athletes frequently display physiological hyperventilation at peak effort, which dissociates respiration from cardiovascular demand. Furthermore, slow ramp-up during initiation of exercise and variable measurements in the presence of lung disease, upper extremity movement, and at high altitude are all drawbacks of using thoracic impedance. Closed loop systems do not share these issues but present their own disadvantages because they offer less functionality that can be optimized.

General principles for rate-response pacing are demonstrated in our presented case (Table 1). First, metabolic-chronotropic mismatch should be minimized. The heart rate-VO2 relationship should remain linear below the VeT and approximate predicted values. In patients with pacemakers that allow VeT programming, a CPET should be performed to accurately account for hyperventilation as well as altered heart rate kinetics beyond the VeT. Second, rate of increase in pacing should be tailored to the patient's exercise-associated symptoms. RFs can be adjusted if rapid increase in exercise intensity is required, whereas sensor reaction time should be used to create gradual drift in heart rate. Similarly, depending on reported patient symptoms, both maximum tracking rate and lower rate can be raised or lowered. Care should be taken to avoid increasing overall burden of atrial pacing, especially unnecessary nocturnal pacing. ## Conclusions

Athletes with PPMs for sinus node dysfunction can be highly symptomatic with exercise. Rate-response pacing sensors with nominal settings do not recapitulate physiological sinus node activity. Tailoring implantable cardiac device function to the highly active patient requires a meticulous approach centered on synchronous maximum effort exercise and device testing guided by patient-reported activity intensity, type, and associated symptoms. Such programming approaches warrant large-scale prospective investigative trials to evaluate pacemaker outcomes in athletes and drive innovations to both hardware and software.Take-Home Messages•Athletes with pacemakers for sinus node dysfunction spend prolonged periods of time at peak effort physiology and can experience a disproportionate degree of symptomatic chronotropic incompetence.•A maximum effort cardiopulmonary exercise test combined with device interrogation, and detailed exercise history, is crucial to identifying target parameters for optimization of rate-response pacing.
